To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the MSLQ subscales Self-Efficacy and Time and Study Environments provided incremental validity for predicting course grades, but only in the high- and medium-ACT groups.

(a) the MSLQ subscales Self-Efficacy, Time and Study Environment and Test Anxiety were the only variables to provide incremental validity for predicting course grade, and (b) when the low, medium and high ACT groups are disaggregated, only the Time and Study Environment subscale provided incremental validity for the low ACT students.

only two of 15 subscales (self-efficacy and time and study environment) of the Motivated Learning Strategies Questionnaire (MSQ) provide incremental validity for predicting course grades, and that only time and study provide incremental validity for the lowest performing ACT students.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: What are the most important variables that predict academic performance, and how do they interact?
the incremental validity of the Motivated Strategy for Learning Questionnaire in predicting academic performance, after the contribution of academic aptitude has been taken into consideration.
the question of whether the Motivated Strategies Questionnaire (MSQ) provides incremental validity in predicting college student performance, over and above the contribution of academic aptitude.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the MSLQ is a valid and reliable measure of student motivation and self- efficacy in academic settings, and that the MSL questionnaire is the most comprehensive of all such instruments.
the MSLQ is a valid measure of student learning motivation and learning strategies.
there is little or no evidence that the MSLQ has incremental predictive validity beyond that provided by ACT scores.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the results of this study indicate that the MSLQ is a valid instrument for predicting academic performance, and that the Self-efficacy subscale, and the Time and Study Environment subscale are particularly useful for predicting grades in college courses.

we have shown that motivation is an important predictor of performance in college, and that it is not just a reflection of cognitive ability, as some have argued (see Lounsbury & Gibson, 2002, for a review).

students' motivation to learn and the strategies they use are not only related to their performance in academic settings but are related to their self-concept, their self-efficacy beliefs, and the goals that they set for themselves.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should be careful not to overestimate the importance of motivation.
the MSLQ is a useful instrument for understanding how students approach their academic tasks.
we need to do a better job of understanding the factors that contribute to students' success in the classroom.
